ops_014:n1.prompt:
You are helping me prepare the internal planning materials needed to define our headcount, budget, and space needs before we start touring offices. This is groundwork only — the actual sizing decision requires my leadership team's judgment on growth forecasts and financial constraints, and that decision-making discussion remains a human step you cannot perform.

Please ask me for any of the following if I haven't already provided them: current headcount, hiring plan/growth forecast for the next 12-24 months, current monthly/annual budget ceiling for rent, preferred location(s) or neighborhoods, and any must-have amenities (parking, meeting rooms, kitchen, etc.).

Once I share what I know, do the following:
1. Draft a simple headcount projection table (current, 6mo, 12mo, 24mo) based on the growth plan I give you.
2. Calculate a suggested square footage range using standard planning ratios (e.g., ~150-250 sq ft per person for a mix of desks, meeting rooms, and common space), showing the math clearly.
3. Draft a budget worksheet estimating monthly rent range (using typical price-per-square-foot ranges for the market I specify, clearly labeled as estimates to verify locally), plus rough estimates for utilities, furniture, and buildout contingency.
4. Compile a one-page "space requirements brief" summarizing headcount, square footage target, budget range, must-haves, and location preferences, ready for me to review with leadership.

Done looks like: a clear headcount table, a square footage estimate with reasoning shown, a budget worksheet, and a one-page brief — all in a format I can paste into a doc or share with my team.

Do not make the final sizing or budget decision yourself — this remains a human step for leadership to discuss and finalize. Report back with the drafted materials and a short list of open questions or assumptions I should confirm with my team before finalizing numbers.

ops_014:n2.prompt:
You are helping me prepare for in-person office space tours with a commercial real estate broker, as part of leasing an office. Physically walking each property with the broker to assess condition and fit remains a human step that you cannot perform — do not attempt to simulate or complete it.

What I need you to prepare instead:

1. Ask me for: my target neighborhood(s)/submarket, headcount and desired square footage range, budget (monthly or per-square-foot), must-have amenities (e.g., parking, elevator, kitchen), lease term preference, and target move-in date.
2. Draft a one-page requirements brief summarizing these criteria, suitable for me to send to the broker.
3. Draft an outreach email to the broker requesting a tour schedule of candidate spaces matching the brief, asking for address, square footage, asking rent, and availability date for each listing.
4. Create a tour-day evaluation checklist/scorecard template (columns: address, size, rent, condition, natural light, layout fit, notes, follow-up questions) that I can fill in on-site or right after each visit.
5. Set up a simple tracking sheet (as a table you output, or instructions for a spreadsheet) listing each property toured, with placeholder rows for date, broker notes, and my rating, so I can log results after each tour.
6. Prepare a list of standard questions to ask at each space (e.g., lease term flexibility, build-out allowances, utilities included, parking availability).

Done looks like: I have the requirements brief, broker outreach draft, evaluation checklist, tracking sheet, and question list ready to use — all clearly labeled and easy to copy into email or print.

Report back with: the drafted brief, email, checklist, tracking sheet, and question list in full text, plus a short note confirming that scheduling and conducting the actual site tours remains a human step for me and the broker to carry out.

ops_014:n3.prompt:
You are helping me compare competing office lease proposals and model the true all-in cost of each so I can pick the best option. Ask me for: (1) the LOIs or proposal documents/terms for each space I'm considering (rent per square foot, square footage, term length, free rent months, tenant improvement allowance, escalation rate, operating expense/CAM structure — full-service, modified gross, or triple net, and any expense stops or base year), (2) my move-in timeline, and (3) any known one-time costs (broker fees I owe directly, moving costs, furniture/cabling estimates, security deposit amount).

With that, build a comparison model in a spreadsheet or document that, for each proposal: (a) calculates gross monthly and annual rent including escalations for the full term, (b) nets out free rent months to get effective rent, (c) subtracts or amortizes the tenant improvement allowance against my estimated buildout cost, (d) adds estimated CAM/operating expenses or triple-net charges based on the stated structure, (e) adds one-time costs (deposit, moving, furniture, cabling), and (f) produces a total effective cost per square foot per year and total cost over the full term, so proposals are compared on equal footing regardless of headline rent.

Flag any proposal with unusual escalation rates, low TI allowances relative to buildout needs, or ambiguous expense language that needs clarification from the landlord or broker.

Done looks like: a clear side-by-side table ranking all proposals by total effective cost and cost per square foot per year, with key assumptions and open questions listed. Report back with the comparison table, your recommended top choice with reasoning, and the list of clarifying questions to send to each landlord or broker before proceeding to negotiation.

ops_014:n4.prompt:
You are helping me prepare to negotiate a Letter of Intent (LOI) for an office lease. The actual back-and-forth negotiation with the landlord's broker remains a human step, but I need you to prepare everything so I walk into it ready.

First, ask me for any missing inputs: target space size (sq ft), city/submarket, asking rent (per sq ft or per month), lease term I want, desired tenant improvement (TI) allowance, any free-rent period I want, exit/termination rights I need (e.g., early termination option, sublease rights, expansion/contraction options), my budget ceiling, comparable market rents if I have them, and any deadlines driving urgency.

Then do the following:
1. Draft a one-page LOI term sheet template covering: base rent (with step-ups), term length, TI allowance, free rent, security deposit/guarantee expectations, renewal options, exit rights, and key contingencies.
2. Prepare a negotiation brief: my target vs. walk-away position on each term (rent, TI, term, exit), and 2-3 fallback positions for each in case the landlord pushes back.
3. If I give you comparable rents or prior offers, summarize them into a short market comparison to support my ask.
4. Draft an email I can send to the broker introducing my opening terms, ready for me to review and send.
5. List open questions I should raise with the broker (e.g., who pays broker commission, landlord's typical TI reimbursement timeline, guarantee requirements).

When done, give me: the term sheet draft, the negotiation brief with fallback positions, the draft broker email, and the open-questions list — clearly labeled and ready for me to use in the actual negotiation, which remains a human step.

ops_014:n5.prompt:
You are helping me manage the 'counsel reviews the lease' step of our office lease process. This is a policy-gate step: an actual attorney must assess and accept the legal risk in the lease (indemnities, personal/corporate guarantee, default clauses, renewal and termination terms). You cannot perform or substitute for that legal judgment — please prepare everything around it and then stop for human sign-off.

First, ask me for anything missing: the lease document (PDF or link), the name/contact of our attorney or law firm handling review, the deal terms I've already negotiated (rent, term, TI allowance, guarantee type, security deposit amount), and any deadline (e.g., LOI expiration or landlord's requested signature date).

Then do the following:
1. Organize and summarize the lease document's key sections (parties, term, rent schedule, guarantee/indemnity language, default/remedies, assignment/subletting, insurance requirements) into a concise briefing memo for counsel, flagging anything that looks like it deviates from the negotiated LOI terms.
2. Draft a clear email to our attorney transmitting the lease, the briefing memo, and our deadline, asking for their written risk assessment and any redline requests.
3. Create a tracking checklist noting: date sent to counsel, expected turnaround, and a placeholder for counsel's verdict (approved / approved with changes / rejected).
4. Since counsel's response will arrive later, note that this step requires periodic polling — check back for their reply and log it when it arrives, but do not attempt to interpret or override their legal risk determination.

When the memo, email draft, and checklist are ready, report back with all three plus a summary of open questions, and stop for human sign-off before sending anything or proceeding to signature.

ops_014:n6.prompt:
You are helping me prepare for signing an office lease and any accompanying guarantee. This is step ops_014:n6 in our office-leasing process, and it is a policy-gate step: signing creates binding legal and financial liability, so only an authorized officer of the company can actually sign — you must never sign, accept terms, approve, or submit any part of this on my behalf.

Please ask me for anything missing: the final negotiated lease document (and guarantee document, if applicable), the identity/title of the authorized signer, the entity name that will be party to the lease, and the e-signature platform or method the landlord/broker is using (e.g., DocuSign, Adobe Sign, or physical signature).

Your job is to prepare everything needed so the human signer can review and sign quickly and correctly:
1. Summarize the key business terms (rent, term length, escalation, security deposit amount, guarantee scope/cap/duration, renewal/termination options) in plain language for a final human sanity check.
2. Flag any clauses that differ from what was agreed in the LOI or lease review, if you have access to prior versions.
3. Pre-fill any signer fields, dates, and entity names in the signature platform draft if that's possible without submitting.
4. Prepare a checklist of what to verify before signing: correct parties named, correct dollar amounts, guarantee terms understood, deposit wiring instructions confirmed, COI requirements noted.
5. Note any deadlines (e.g., lease expiration of offer) so the human signer knows the timeline.

Once this packet (summary, flagged discrepancies, pre-filled draft, checklist, deadlines) is ready, stop for human sign-off. Report back with the summary, any flagged issues, the checklist, and confirmation that the document is staged and ready for the authorized signer to review and execute themselves.

ops_014:n7.prompt:
You are helping me wire the security deposit for our new office lease using {{vendor}}, our startup banking platform. Before starting, ask me for: (1) the landlord or property management company's legal name and wiring instructions (bank name, account number, routing/SWIFT details) as stated in the signed lease, (2) the exact deposit amount and currency, (3) any reference/memo text the landlord requires (e.g., lease ID, suite number), and (4) which teammate should approve the payment if our workflow requires dual sign-off.

Once you have these details, log into {{vendor}} using my configured credentials and: search for the landlord as a vendor/payee (or set them up as a new payee if they don't exist yet), enter the wire payment with the correct amount, currency, and memo, and select wire as the payment method. Check and show me the delivery time estimate before confirming anything. If our account has an approval workflow enabled, route the payment through it to the designated approver rather than sending it yourself. Do not click a final one-click send/approve action that irreversibly moves funds — that decision remains a human step, so stop for human sign-off once the payment is fully filled out and ready to send.

When done, report back: the payee name and account details entered, the amount and memo, the delivery estimate shown, whether it was routed to an approver or is awaiting my confirmation, and a screenshot or transaction reference number if available.

ops_014:n8.prompt: You are helping me get a certificate of insurance (COI) issued to our new landlord using Embroker, our commercial insurance provider. Before starting, ask me for anything you don't already have: (1) the landlord's exact legal entity name and mailing address as it should appear as 'additional insured' and 'certificate holder', (2) the leased property's address, (3) our company name as insured on the policy, and (4) any specific coverage limits or additional-insured wording the lease requires (check the lease review notes or ask me if unsure). Then log into our Embroker account using my configured credentials and navigate to the certificate of insurance request or self-service COI form. Fill in the landlord as certificate holder and additional insured with the details I provided, referencing our existing policy. Generate the COI, and if Embroker allows sending it directly to a recipient, prepare the send with the landlord's contact email if I've given it to you — otherwise download the generated COI. Do not submit or send anything until I confirm the details are correct; this step involves issuing an official insurance document, so please stop for human sign-off before finalizing or transmitting it to the landlord. Report back with: confirmation that the COI was successfully generated in Embroker, the exact additional-insured/certificate-holder wording used, a copy or link to the draft COI, and whether it was sent or is awaiting my review and send. Flag any missing policy data, form errors, or required fields that blocked completion.

ops_014:n9.prompt:
You are helping me set up internet, utilities, and building access for our newly leased office. Before starting, ask me for anything you need that isn't already known: the office's full street address and suite number, our lease start/move-in date, company legal name and billing entity, preferred internet speed/tier or use case (headcount, VoIP, etc.), our current utility providers (or ask me to confirm which electric/gas/water provider serves that address), and the property management or landlord contact info for building access setup.

Then do the following:
1. Research and identify the internet service providers that serve the specific address (search provider coverage-checker tools online) and shortlist 2-3 options with plans matching our needs.
2. Identify the local electric/gas/water utility provider(s) for that address if not already provided.
3. For each provider (internet and utilities), go to their official sign-up page and complete the new-service/business account application using our company details and configured credentials, selecting the move-in date as the desired activation date. Fill in all required fields (billing address, contact person, plan selection).
4. For building access, draft an email to the property manager/landlord requesting the process for issuing key fobs, access cards, or codes for our team, referencing our lease and move-in date.
5. Track confirmation numbers, scheduled installation/activation dates, and any documents or photo IDs each provider requires, compiling them into a single checklist.

Do not submit any payment authorization, sign contracts, or agree to terms on my behalf — pause and stop for human sign-off before finalizing any application that requires a signature, deposit payment, or credit check.

Report back with: providers selected, application/confirmation status for each, scheduled install dates, the access-request email draft, and any items still pending my review or signature.
